vignette:
Malia was sixty-three, a project manager who had spent decades keeping complex timelines on track, and she had never imagined her own body would become the project that failed. Two years ago, what began as a routine gallbladder surgery turned into a nightmare: a postoperative infection that spiraled into septic shock. She spent three weeks in the intensive care unit, her bed surrounded by machines that beeped and dripped, her veins filled with lines and tubes. Twice the medical team told her husband she might not make it. Malia survived, but the memory of those weeks had not passed—it had lodged inside her like a second infection. Because the memory returned so vividly and without warning, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in the beep of a microwave, in the smell of hand sanitizer, in the way a fluorescent light flickered overhead. At unpredictable moments, the memory would return not as a recollection but as a full sensory reliving: she could feel the fever heat crawling up her neck, hear the high-pitched alarm of a monitor, smell the antiseptic and the faint metallic tang of blood. In these moments, her body would curl automatically into the same fetal position she had held on the worst night, her knees drawn up, her arms pressed against her chest. She could not put any of it into words; when her husband asked what she was experiencing, the story dissolved before she could speak.

After she was discharged, Malia tried to return to her life. She went back to managing her team, but she found herself snapping at colleagues for small mistakes, her irritability flaring without warning. Her concentration frayed; she would stare at spreadsheets and see only the pattern of IV tubing. At home, when her husband touched her shoulder from behind, she would gasp and pull away, her heart hammering. She knew these reactions were excessive, but she could not stop them. What frightened her most was the shame that had taken root: she felt humiliated by what her body had done—how it had failed her, how it had nearly killed her. She had come to believe that her life was destroyed, that she could no longer trust her own body to keep her alive. That belief made her hypersensitive to any reminder of her illness. A colleague mentioning a routine checkup sent a spike of dread through her chest, and she would steer the conversation elsewhere. When she saw a needle in a doctor’s office waiting room—just a glimpse through a glass door—her stomach turned and she left without making an appointment. She postponed her own follow-up medical exam for over a year, certain that another test would uncover another betrayal.

The memories and the shame fed each other. Each intrusive reliving confirmed to Malia that her body was fundamentally unreliable, and that conviction made the next memory more vivid—she could almost feel the wound drain again. The constant threat of a trigger kept her on edge; her irritability shortened her fuse at work, and the stress of that itself seemed to summon another memory, as if her nervous system had learned a single, punishing rhythm. Feeling this constantly on edge, Malia had come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering—that she was fundamentally broken. She began avoiding conversations about health with her closest friends, and she stopped attending social gatherings where a casual remark might undo her. Her husband grew frustrated, unable to understand why she flinched from his touch or why she would not discuss a future retirement trip that required a plane ride—“What if I get sick again?” she would say, unable to finish the thought.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a moment that forced the cycle out into the open. A minor urinary tract infection sent her to urgent care, and the sight of the nurse’s gloved hands reaching for a syringe triggered a full-blown panic attack in the examination room. She fled, embarrassed and shaking, and called her husband from the parking lot. Sitting in her car, she realised that her life had indeed shrunk—not because of the trauma itself, but because of the fortress she had built around it. She was afraid of what she might become if she kept going this way, but she was equally afraid that therapy would force her to remember the very sensations she had spent two years trying to outrun. She did not know if she could talk about the illness without reliving it, but she knew she could not keep living as she was.
